tier_reason: README shows first-party timings against zlib inflate 1.2.11 on two inputs, with no benchmark harness, CPU, compiler or flags stated, so C.

corrections.workload: Decompress a zlib stream of a large raw texture (60,132,846 bytes compressed to 25,614,357) and a gzip archive (147,120,395 bytes compressed to 53,625,384), memory to memory; time in microseconds.
corrections.claimed_speedup: zlib bitstream: zlib inflate 1.2.11 134,245 us (100%); Inflate++ with checksum 118,399 us (91%); without checksum 110,238 us (85%). gzip bitstream: zlib 465,567 us (100%); Inflate++ with checksum 362,133 us (87%); without checksum 265,462 us (65%). About 1.13x (zlib) and 1.29x (gzip) faster with checksum, 1.22x and 1.75x without (derived from page data).
corrections.caveats: No CPU, compiler, flags or benchmark harness; two inputs only. The README's percentage column does not match its own times (e.g. 362,133/465,567 is 78%, not 87%; 265,462/465,567 is 57%, not 65%), so the table was edited carelessly. The 'without checksum' rows skip verification that zlib performs, so they are not like-for-like. Baseline zlib 1.2.11 is old; zlib-ng and libdeflate are far faster than both. Windows-only build script; no tests in repo.

notes: Numbers match the README times exactly; the record's derived 1.1-1.15x understated the gzip case, corrected. Metadata checked: MIT, 22 stars, not fork/archived, last commit 2021-03-08 (abandoned).

tier_reason: doc/README.benchmarks is the author's own table against 7z, xz, bzip2 and gzip with CPU named but no compiler, flags or benchmark scripts, so C.

corrections.hardware: 3GHz quad-core Intel Core2, 8GB RAM, SSD, lrzip v0.612 (kernel tarball and 10GB VM image tables); 2.53GHz dual-core Core2, 4GB, 32-bit userspace, lrzip v0.5.1 (six-kernel-tree table); i7-3930K 3.2GHz, 32GB (10GB image vs gzip/pbzip2)
corrections.caveats: Old (Core2-era, document dated 7 July 2012) numbers in one doc file, no compiler, flags or scripts. Wall-time comparison with lrzip using all cores against xz of that era (single-threaded) and 7z. Modern multithreaded xz (-T) and zstd --long would narrow or reverse the gap. Author's own benchmark. lrzip is a file-level CLI (rzip long-range pass plus LZMA/LZO/ZPAQ backends), 64-bit only, and wins mostly on large inputs with long-distance redundancy.

notes: All claimed numbers found in doc/README.benchmarks; added the 10GB image table and dates. Metadata: GPL-2.0, 704 stars, last commit 2026-09-21 (active).

tier_reason: README gives the author's 7-Zip-plugin run on Matt Mahoney's 10GB corpus against LZMA, with no CPU, compiler or flags; the independent LTCB/MOC results it links could not be opened (mattmahoney.net EGRESS_BLOCKED), so C.

corrections.caveats: Results are the author's own run with the 32-bit 7-Zip 9.38 LZHAM plugin; CPU, compiler and flags not stated. Repo is the 'unstable/experimental' v1.1 devel branch; stable v1.0 lives in github.com/richgel999/lzham_codec. README says LZHAM is now public domain while the LICENSE file is MIT. Test time includes archive overhead rather than pure decode. README itself says the decoder is slower than zlib and only beats LZMA above roughly 1-13 KB of compressed input. Code unchanged since 2015; later commits only edit the README.

notes: README numbers match the record exactly (223.050/71.292 s is 3.1x, derived). Metadata: MIT LICENSE, 82 stars, not archived, last commit 2023-05-14 (README only), abandoned. Independent LTCB entry might support B if a later retier can reach mattmahoney.net.
